newsitem.title: FRANCE: Galliano stages parade at Dior ready-to-wear show.
newsitem.headline: Galliano stages parade at Dior ready-to-wear show.

text.p: Swashbuckling British designer John Galliano let loose his first ready-to-wear collection for the house of Christian Dior on Tuesday.
The bobby socks, purple platform shoes and curvy suits reminescent of the label's landmark "new look" came with micro miniskirts so short they exposed the models' underwear.
Galliano discarded blouses, replacing them with Masai necklaces of pearls or filigreed silver while Obi bows or Japanese combs ornamented hats and handbags.

Chinese-style dresses with Ming collars were the pillar of this collection, whether in pastel angora fringed with silver beads, or stretchy jacquard in candy colours like lilac and canary yellow. There was also red or gold necktie silk with skirts sculpted from the signature Dior bow.
The collection was yet another example of the 36-year-old designer's exuberant creativity and the trouble he has with channelling it towards clothes for the shop-rack and not the couture salon.
But in terms of sheer excitement the show was a triumph.

The evening wear was sensuous and stunning, sinewy bias-cut black gowns handpainted with orchids and lined with plum satin and fringed opium-den dresses. One of the most striking pieces was an aqua crepe de chine column swirling with floral embroidery.
For a finale, Galliano marched out the likes of Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell and a brunette Claudia Schiffer in glimmering red dragon-lady outfits.
Earlier, Dries Van Noten took the fashion crowd down the legendary Silk Road, mingling the shimmering silks of a Chinese courtesan with the rough-hewn wool of a Tibetan shepherd.

The Belgian designer married rustic quilted cotton coats with richly patterned kimono silk pareos, drab wool kaftans with gold-embroidered scarves, or glimmering velveteen columns with alpaca jackets.

The line was long and layered as if the supermodels were getting ready for a bitter Himalayan winter, but the dreary shades were sometimes brightened. For instance, a heavy coat flapped open, revealing its stunning persimmon lining shot with gold flowers, or a burnished shawl was wound around the waist of a dark kaftan and tied with gold cord.
"The colours were magnificent and the clothes were so comfortable and free of aggression," enthused boutique-owner Maria Luisa.

"In Milan and London I saw so many shows with hard, violent, clothes. Very 1980s. But Van Noten is always true to himself: the layering, the strong ethnic flavour. It's a poetic journey, but clothes that any woman can wear."
One British fashion critic was more ambivalent. "Beautiful, but depressing" was the verdict.

On Monday night, Van Noten's fellow citizen and former classmate Dirk Bikkembergs sent out an understated collection while Swiss designer Bertrand Marechal drew his inspiration from suburban drug addicts.
Bikkembergs unleashed a marathon of dark, asymetrically cut jackets over slacks, whose waistlines sloped under the navel, giving supermodels' bellies a few extra ounces.
